paragraphs.text: If everyone could please quiet down so we can get started.
Thank you everyone for coming here today. If we can be quiet please so we can continue.
Thank you. We're glad that all of you could be here today. This- Just- if you can be quiet, please, so we can continue.

Just a warning, if we cannot continue our uh work session meeting today, we will be moved to an alternative location. This public regular meeting of the Board of Education for November 17th, 2026 is called to order. All items being considered this evening are posted on PPS website on the board and meetings tab. This meeting is being replayed and streamed on PPS YouTube page, uh also replayed on Channel 28. Good evening and welcome.

Tonight's meeting is being held at Benson Auditorium to accommodate the larger audience. Uh before we get started, just a few reminders. Uh we have again been reminded by the fire marshal that we must keep the aisles and walkways clear. In order to keep from exceeding the occupancy level, we will require that everyone take a seat. Uh, once we reach maximum capacity, the doors will close, uh, not allowing anyone to enter unless you're signed up for public comment.

If you're outside and did not get a seat and you have signed up for public comment, uh, please notify a staff member who will let you in. Uh, we also ask that you be considerate to those around you and keep any signs below chin level. I want to acknowledge that we have a large crowd tonight because this topic is very important to all of us. Uh, the only time our board can work through these topics ask questions of one another and staff are in our meetings that have uh that are conducted in public. What that means is that distractions from- Please stop.

What that means is distractions from the audience can prohibit us from working on this issue that is important enough to be here uh for this evening. If this happens, we will be recessing one time. If it continues to happen, we will be moving to an alternative space and the meeting will become virtual. So uh this is the same same protocols and expectations as what's in city halls, our state legislature. We welcome, we're glad that you're here, uh but we also need time to conduct our business.

So thank you. First off, we're gonna start off with general public comment, and I would like to start with our students first. First, uh before we begin, just wanna review guidelines for our public comment. First, the board thanks you for taking the time to attend this meeting and provide your public comments. Public input, especially from our students, helps inform us and improves our work.

We look forward to hearing your thoughts and reflections. As board members, we are here to listen and not engage in conversation with those who are testifying. Our board office may follow up on board-related issues raised during public testimony. We also request that complaints about individual employees be directed to the superintendent's office as a personnel matter. I will remind PPS staff who are giving public comment that they may not provide testimony about students that could violate confidentiality protections under FERPA.

This includes testimony using information that could identify students, especially in their school community, by use of direct or indirect linkages such as school grades, special education, or other status. For materials you'd like the board to receive, such as handouts, pictures, please email those to school to schoolboard@pps.net. When you come up and give your public comment, be sure to clearly state your name, spell your last name. Today you'll have 2 minutes to speak. Uh when the orange light goes off, that means you have 30 seconds, and when the red light goes off, that means please end your comments.

For the sake of time, we will be enforcing that strictly today. Uh so first off, let's start off with our students. Ms. Powell, can you um call up the students actually, we have students who signed up, correct? Yes, we do. We have 3: Wren Waddell, Adams Jacollier, and Collins Jacolier.

Hello, my name is Wren Waddell, and I am a second grader at Creston Elementary School. Thank you for letting me speak today. My question is, why would anybody want to go to Creston? Creston is a really good science school. STEAM days are when teachers and parents teach us about special science projects.
Questen is the only school with STEAM days, and if it closes, no more STEAM days. Does anybody know why Questen is closing? Thank you.
Thank you.

Hello, my name is Adams Jackolger, and I am a 4th grader at Lewis Elementary. I would rather be- I would rather be watching a movie on my couch under a heated blanket than speaking in front of all these people on live TV. I am here to say that you should not close Lewis. If you close Lewis, You will not just be closing a school, you will be closing a strong and inclusive community. There are a number of reasons why you should not close Lewis.

One reason is that Lewis is earthquake safe. It is also ADA accessible. Another reason is that a lot of my teachers might not keep teaching us. At Lewis, me and my first grade brother walk to school every day by ourselves because it is safe to walk and is really close. If you close Lewis, we won't be able to walk to school.

If we get moved to Dunaway, lots of kids will have to cross 39th to get to Dunaway. 39Th is a very busy and dangerous street for kids to cross alone. Before I started kindergarten, Lewis got students from a bigger area. Our school used to have 2 to 3 classes per grade before the boundary changed. If we got our old boundary back, our school would be bigger and would be more diverse.

On Fridays, I get out of bed really fast because I have Safety Patrol and Compass Coaching. Compass Coaching is when you are a recess monitor for the K-2 kids. Our PE teacher, Mr. D, teaches us how to be leaders during Compass Coaching. Here's some other fun facts. Our plumbing is updated.

Our neighborhood has lots of new houses and young families. You should vote for a scenario that makes our boundary bigger again and will fill Lewis. It will keep us in a safe and accessible school the money people already spent won't be wasted. More Portland children will be safer, closer to their homes, and have the things they need to learn. In conclusion, the Lewis community is strong, academically successful, inclusive, and won't stop fighting to keep our school open.
Thank you.
Ms. Fowl, do we have any other students signed up today?
Sharmika Schuster and Isabelle Johnson. Thank you.

Yeah, go ahead. Sharmika Schuster, S-C-H-U-S-T-E-R. I speak to you tonight strictly as a private citizen and concerned neighbor. This photo is me at age 5 at Peninsula Elementary. Growing up in that building deeply shaped the foundation of my life.

Statistics on health disparities, race, ethnicity, and education access cause a sharp divide in our society. Society. Treating our neighborhood schools like a line item you can just wipe away to remove a $65 million deficit won't work. Cost analysis shows that there will be more trauma and more expense in closing the inner city schools like Peninsula than there will be compared to the more affluent schools that have resources to mitigate these issues. You aren't actually eliminating a deficit, you're just shifting it to our healthcare system.

Tearing a hole in the Kenton community By closing, Peninsula and other schools may inflict deep, lasting trauma on these children. When you combine poverty, childhood trauma, and displacement, it physically wrecks the human body. Years down the road, the fallout may manifest as lifelong health problems. High blood pressure, soaring addictions, strokes, diabetes, kidney disease, heart failure- these are just a few of the conditions I've treated throughout my career. And I have seen the devastating fallout.

Once that kind of damage is done, the healthcare system can't just fix it. By closing these schools, you aren't saving money, you're just multiplying a bill that taxpayers are gonna have to pay later, and the healthcare system. I speak to you tonight not just as a neighbor, but as a double board-certified nurse practitioner with a master's in public health and global health disparities. I get what this trauma will do. I graduated Howard, OHSU, and later Penn.

Closing these schools will deprive these children of the same opportunities. Instead of closing Peninsula and other schools, follow proven models like Cincinnati and New York City by leveraging state and federal grants to co-locate wraparound services like food pantries, housing navigators, ESL, etc.
Thank you.
Do I go? Uh, yes, please. Thank you. Thank you. Uh, Isabel Johnson, J-O-H-N-S-O-N.

I'm very nervous. I'm uh the Mount Tabor Middle School PTA president, but I'm here speaking tonight as a parent of an 8th grader. I'm here actually to commend the board and Dr. Armstrong for taking on this incredibly unpopular work. Of trying to ensure that all of our students have access to well-resourced schools. I know that you're going against the grain, that this is so incredibly unpopular, but we have declining enrollment, we have declining birth rates, and we can't outrun that.
And the state is not coming to save us. Can you please refrain from booing and hissing, please? And that's totally fine. I totally get you're gonna boo and hiss. And I'm, you know, go for it.

Um, but I really feel that if we do not face this now, we're just gonna revisit it next year or the year after. And I'm here-. Can you please stop interrupting? I'm here specifically to voice support for middle schools and libraries. When my son was at Glencoe Elementary, I remember wishing it was a K-8.

But I've watched him grow from a nervous 6th grader to a confident 8th grade web leader. And it's really changed how I think about middle school. I think the band program is one of the most amazing things about Tabor. But for my son, one of the biggest benefits has simply been being around more kids. Libraries.

I volunteered in Glencoe's library for 6 years and now volunteer at Tabor. I see firsthand how much students love library time. Access to books is fundamental to literacy, yet year after year, funding cuts have reduced that access. In this age of misinformation and disinformation, librarians and libraries matter more than ever. As part of our right-sized schools, please give our students fully staffed libraries open every day.
Thank you. Thank you.
Can you call the next big signal?

Uh, I understand the energy in here is great. I appreciate that you're here and things like that, but we have people who are here to give public comment. I also Asking people to refrain also from clapping is because it may shorten people's time in public comment as well. The other thing is also hissing and booing, and even clapping can also put chilling effect on free speech, as we are here to welcome all ideas and all thoughts so that people have a time to share. So we please ask people to refrain from any comments, cheering, booing, hissing during public comment.

Let's be respectful to each other. Our kids are watching, and we need to be open to all ideas, even if they're not aligned with our own. So thank you. Uh, Ms. Powell, can you call the next two? Sahan Mekelbe and Sam Barroso.
Okay, I'll go first. Good evening, my name is Sam Barroso. I'm the parent of a 3rd grader and and kindergartner at Sabin. First, thank you for what you're doing. This is hard work.

I see you. I moved to Sabin because I wanted my children to have what my parents gave me, a diverse, strong public education. Sabin is whiter than I expected, but we're also a community of Black, Native, Latino, and many, many mixed-race babies. So when I talk about our community, I ask that you not erase us, but see us for our complexity. Sabin is where my third grader experienced her first Black Excellence Night, something she never had at her previous school.

Now, my life's work is rooted in equity, and I will say the recommendation for Sabin is a clumsy brute force approach to equity when what is needed is intentionality. It disregards what it means to be just one of 3 SES schools in the district. And what pains me is that after years of raising concerns to the district, it took tragedies for the district to finally pay attention to what an SES school needs. I had hoped we'd learn from that. What Sabin has learned is that it needs resources, it needs focus.

It cannot be one program among many. I fought hard for Sabin, and at this point I do expect it to close, but that doesn't mean the path forward makes sense. Not yet. Move our entire school community, including SCS, wholly together where there is space. Build one stronger school from two similar communities rather than overcrowding us at MLK with three programs competing for support, resources, and space: the Mandarin DLI, the English Scholars, and our SCS program.

Merge Sabin with Irvington. This is a more manageable transition for the district, and it preserves a neighborhood school in the inner northeast. Don't make inner northeast a private school enclave. This is not- and I want to say, this is not about sending Sabin to Grant or reversing last year's board decision. It is about finding the most stable path forward for our kids.

My address is zoned for Jeff. I'm proud of this. My address should be remained zoned for Jeff, even if my children go to Irvington. This is the path of least resistance. You need this because in 2 years you'll have to revisit our very gerrymandered boundaries alongside a full review of our schools, and then we can talk about boundary changes while we're not at the same time asking to close our schools.
I'll just close with one sentence: equity deserves more than a blunt instrument. It deserves thoughtfulness that brings us along together on this journey.

Thank you. If you do run out- this goes for everybody- if you do run out of time and the alarm goes off, you're please- you're free- welcome actually to email it to the school board. Uh, and we do read all- at least I do read all the emails and it takes forever. But anyways, thank you.

Good evening, good people. My name is Sahan McKelvey. I am the director of advocacy and engagement for Self-Enhancement Inc. SEI. For 45 years, SEI has partnered with Portland Public Schools to support student success, family engagement, workforce development, and wraparound services. Tonight, I'm here to support Dr. Kimberly Armstrong.

First, I want to acknowledge the very real grief and concern being expressed by school communities. These are difficult decisions that affect students, families, educators, and neighborhoods that care deeply about our schools. At the same time, we must confront the reality that PPS is facing continued enrollment declines that will are projected to continue moving forward, a projected $65 million budget shortfall, and a portfolio of buildings designed for serving students, twice as many students as what the district now serves. Maintaining underutilized facilities is not the same as maximizing student opportunity. What I appreciate about this recommendation is that it is ultimately not about closing schools.

It's about creating stronger schools. Most importantly-. Stop, please. Students who have historically faced the greatest barriers stand to benefit the most. Students experiencing poverty, multilingual learners, and students receiving special education services will all see dramatically improved access to sustainable schools under Dr. Armstrong's plan.

I want to recognize the leadership of Dr. Kimberly Armstrong. She did not create these enrollment declines. She did not create the demographic shifts that caused them. She did not create the fiscal challenges facing PPS right now. Stop interrupting, please.

She didn't create the budget deficit. She inherited these things, and now she is charged with fixing a problem that she didn't create. The final recommendation reflects substantial changes made in response to community feedback, born from Dr. Armstrong spending multiple hours making hundreds of site visits to listen to community. Thank you. Doing nothing was never a responsible option.
That's a drop in place. And while these decisions are painful-. We are at time. Sustainable schools and improved opportunities for students is what our goal should be. Right.
SCI supports Dr. Armstrong. Thank you. Thank you.
Ms. Powell, can you call the next 2?

I'm gonna give you one more warning. If anyone interrupts any- public commenter, we are going to take a recess, period. Okay, this is the last warning. It is disrespectful to interrupt our public commenters, whether you agree or disagree. Again, same, also not cheering and hissing or booing, please.

Ms. Powell, can you call the next two? Just add, you were interpreting the time up as the school bell. Just a reminder, the school bell is what went off, not the timer for the speaker. A lot of you seem to think that it was the timer for the speaker, so just making sure you know that. Can you call the next 2?
Ashley Mori and Emma Myers.

My name is Ashley Mori. I'm a PPS parent. Over the past month, the community members have been telling the district and the board that Scenario A and B are incomplete, impractical, based on faulty data, and ultimately harmful to our communities, including our most marginalized communities. In many listening sessions many of you sitting up there committed not to vote for an unsupported, hasty plan without a shot of being well implemented. You told us, wait for the final proposal, the district will meaningfully incorporate your feedback.
Well, the final proposal has been released, and we are here to tell you that the same problems remain.

I have no doubt that you will hear about each and every issue with the final proposal over the next month. So I want to talk to you about governance. As the school board, you are the body responsible for oversight of the Portland School District. This means that you must take the time to seriously vet these proposals, ensure your questions are answered in full, and refuse to support any proposal that does not ensure better outcomes. You may believe that the data supports the district's proposal.
It does not. You may believe that research shows that school closures are positive. It does not. You may believe that your role is to defer to the superintendent. It is not.

You are meant to have independent oversight of the district for the benefit of the public. I am here to urge you to take your oversight role seriously and to hold the superintendent to the highest possible standard, because what she is proposing is drastic, unprecedented, and has a substantial likelihood of causing irreparable harm. Good governance and voting in favor of the district's proposal are mutually exclusive. I urge you to vote no, allow time for legislative reform, and to send the district back to the drawing board to bring forth a serious plan to improve public education outcomes in Portland. Thank you.
Thank you.

Hi, my name is Emma Meyers, M-E-Y-E-R-S. I'm a parent at Rose City Park, and I'm speaking on behalf of our English scholars and the Vietnamese Dual Language Immersion. The district has committed to data-driven equitable decisions. This proposal broke that commitment in two ways. First, closing RCP would dismantle our VDLI program.

The plan to move VDLI to Vestal rests on inaccurate data. VDLI needs 12 classrooms, one English and one Vietnamese teacher for every grade. We understand that facilities told Vestal we only needed 6, which is all they have available. If DLI seat counts are truly unchanged as stated in the final proposal, that means up to 52 students per classroom. It does not add up.

I urge the board tonight to ask how the district intends to address this. Vestal's special educational services, including occupational therapy and life skills, as well as its projected enrollment growth, would compete with VDLI for ADA accessible space. We are the only K-5 school on this list above the district's own 360-student sustainable benchmark. Over 54% of our students are BIPOC. Splitting this community and sending historically underrepresented students to a building that can't hold their- program is unacceptable.

Second, the seismic funding. Voters approved a bond promising retrofits for the riskiest schools. RCP was selected in part because of our high enrollment. Beverly Cleary is receiving the exact same upgrade, and the district is keeping its promise to them. A predominantly white, more affluent school with fewer K-5 students.

We want all students to be safe. But why are you breaking that promise to RCP, a majority BIPOC school with 6 times as many students who qualify for free and reduced lunch? Please examine the real-world impact of this proposal. Moving VDLI effectively dismantles it. Stand by your word.
Apply the same equitable formula to every school and keep RCP's retrofit funded. Thank you.
Ms. Powell, can you call the next 2?
Ms. Powell, can you call the next 2? Oh, that's it? Sorry, I couldn't hear. No worries. Natalia Hirt and Steven Collin.

My name is Natalia, and I have a kindergartner at Rose City Park in the Vietnamese immersion program. Keeping Rose City Park open is what's best for Portland. Tonight I'll focus on one reason why: the expansion of the Ellington, a large affordable family housing complex down the street from our school. The city of Portland bought the Ellington to keep families in our neighborhood. Nearly all of these 260+ units are sized for families, and dozens of them attend Rose City Park.

The Ellington is set for a 4-phase expansion, bringing its number of units to up to 450. This year, Congresswoman Maxine Dexter helped secure $2 million for that expansion. Rose City Park helped establish a walking school bus that gets children safely from the Ellington to school every morning. If we close, that walk goes from 0.8 miles to 1.8 miles, and absenteeism increases. To quote Home Forward, closing Rose City Park Elementary would be devastating for these families.

The school's proximity, partnership, and comprehensive support have helped children attend school, complete their schoolwork, and succeed, unquote. Rose City Park is asking for consistency. Apply the same criteria to us that you've used to keep other schools open, such as enrollment and nearby housing development. Rose City Park and Beverly Cleary have nearly identical seismic upgrades scheduled, yet you cite theirs as a reason for staying open and ours as a reason for closure. We, we are one of 7 K-5 schools in Portland with over 400 and will remain over the 360-student threshold for at least another decade.

Our unique capacity and location fit the long-term vision you've described for Portland schools. If PPS sells Rose City Park, it may never again secure such a sizable plot in modern-day Portland. Moving forward with our seismic upgrade is a smart, safe bet. Everything else is a risk and ultimately a mistake. Look at our demographics, which includes more low-income students than many Title One schools.
And you'll see that closing us hurts the very students this plan is meant to protect. Keeping Rose City Park open is best for East Portland and all of PPS. Thank you. Thank you.

I'm Steven Colivan, C-O-L-I-V-A-N. Families want well-resourced schools. So does PPS. I'm an architect with nearly 2 decades of experience, and I'm here as a Creston parent to ask one question: does it fit? Answering that doesn't take an elaborate spreadsheet.

Count the classrooms, subtract the rooms needed for required programs. What's left is homerooms available. Atkinson has 24 classrooms. 8 Are needed for programs, 4 for special education, plus art, music, ESL, and intervention. That leaves 16 homerooms.

PPS projects 474 students in the fall of '27. At PPS's own average class size, that's 18 homerooms- 2 short. At PPS's own rating for classrooms like Atkinson, 4 short. At PPS's own design standard, 8 short. Room size matters for learning too.

PPS recommends 1,200 square feet for kinder rooms. Atkinson has 900, Creston 1,200. As an architect, I know no building is perfect and compromise is expected. We design every house for Thanksgiving dinner if budget allows. When we can't, we design for weeknight dinners plus a few guests.

But even the leanest version of this plan leaves the kids' table out in the rain. Programs pushed into hallways or inadequate spaces, and learning pays the price. The analysis I'm leaving you tonight shows that Atkinson- and shows you the work for Atkinson and cites every PPS source. PPS answers the same question of does it fit with one word: yes. Our kids deserve more than a checkbox.
Before you vote, require a test fit for every receiving school. Not a spreadsheet, a floor plan sharing where each class and program goes. Then we will all know, does it fit? Thank you.
Thank you.
Ms. Fowl, can you call the Uh, next 2.
Amara Callahan and Laura Westwood.

I'm Amara Callahan, C-A-L-L-A-H-A-N. My daughter Addie asked if she might speak for our schools. I'm a 5th grader at Beach. I matter to Beach and Beach matters to me. Never has our school motto felt more meaningful, yet right now it feels like we don't matter to the district at all.

Please reject the North Portland right-sizing recommendation and and protect Beach Elementary and neighborhood Spanish DLI at Seton, James John, Beach, and Oakleigh Green, where my older sister goes now and where I'm excited to join her next year. Beach isn't just a building to us, it is our second home. I've had the privilege of learning in a DLI program created for Spanish-speaking students with extraordinary teachers from Chile, Mexico, and Spain, and building friendships with Latino kids in our neighborhood. Even though I'm moving on to sixth grade, grade next year. Closing Beach would leave a heartbreaking hole in our community.

It hurts that neither the superintendent nor a single board member has visited us since putting Beach on the closure list. If you came, you would see teachers and staff who love and support each other like family, and a Title One school with academic growth and attendance higher than the district average. Moving our neighborhood kids to a non-Title One school risks taking away vital supports from students who need them most. I have been so excited to go to Oakleigh Green next year, to stay in my neighborhood, walk and bike to school safely, and finally go to school with my friends from Chief Joe. Moving Spanish Immersion 4 miles away to George forces kids like me to choose between the language program we love and the community we belong to, right when our growing brains need that safety net most.

Worse, the numbers don't add up. Only 40% of Oakleigh DLI families say they would go to George. Combining the 42% who stay with incoming students from Phoebian pushes Oakleigh Green over 600 students, well past its true capacity and the 500-student threshold. And DLI shrinks, just like Bridger to Lent. Similarly, if only half of Beach DLI students go to Chavez, Chief Joe risks severe overcrowding.

Please come meet our amazing Beach community. Listen to our voices and how we plan to grow enrollment and invest in public education. I urge you to keep keep our neighborhood schools and DLI pathways intact. Thank you for listening. Gracias por escucharnos.
Thank you.

Good evening. I'm Laura Westwood, W-E-S-T-W-O-O-D. an Irvington and Tubman parent. One thing underlies every decision this board is making: trust. PPS is asking us to trust you as you reshape public education. Trust has to be earned, and right now you have work to do.

The bond audit identified significant financial oversight failures. Revelations about district business conducted over Signal raised serious questions about transparency, Please expand the independent inquiry to include board members. All must be accountable. Then there is community engagement. Last week, not a single board member attended the Latino listening session.

At Irvington, Director DePass scheduled a midday listening session. Parents took time off work. She did not show up. She has not apologized or rescheduled. You cannot ask- families to trust a process while failing to show up and listen.

The decision-making itself raises questions. Rose City Park and Buckman face closure in part because of their seismic scores, yet Beverly Cleary, with the worst seismic score, is slated for retrofit while Irvington is proposed for closure. How can we trust a process based on inconsistent rationale? Fairness also means how you bring communities together. These decisions aren't just about buildings, they're about people.

Treat these as true mergers, not receiving schools and closing schools. That means equitable staff representation, a shared identity, and a new name. You cannot build a new community by erasing half of it. When families lose trust, some leave. We lose students, enrollment, and the funding that follows.

We cannot right-size our way to sustainability while driving families away. Do not vote to advance this process until you can demonstrate consistent criteria, genuine community engagement, and a transparent, fully funded plan for the impacts on students, staff, and communities. These decisions will shape Portland schools for generations. Our communities deserve a process worthy of the consequences. Thank you.
Thank you.

All right, next up, next up we have, we have comments from our union partners. I believe Amy Silvia from the Service Employees International Union has signed up as well. I believe Alicia Chavez, president of PAT, is also Here. And do we have anyone else, Ms. Powell?
Elizabeth Powell. Okay, thank you.
Hello, hello, my name is Amy Sylvia. I'm a mom of two PPS graduates, a registered voter, and the lunch lady at Maplewood Elementary.

I am here today to speak on behalf of SEIU Local 140 custodial and nutrition services. We work across all PPS schools. We believe in our schools and see ourselves as a big part of the community. We are very disappointed in the district decision-making, whether it is big raises for top admin, communication with lack of transparency, or lack of trust we have in the district implementing whatever decisions come out of this process. We want to highlight a few thoughts.

Last year I was on the bargaining team and the district said that it could only afford 1% raises to frontline workers and couldn't pay nutrition services for the Christmas holiday. Boo. Yet the district somehow found money to give superintendent a 3% raise, retention bonuses, retirement annuity, nearly double monthly car stipend, and more. To be told we get 1% and no more, and then for the board to offer up over triple that is a bitter pill for district workers to swallow. We also don't like the spending millions on shady contracts and a closure plan that makes our community sick.

Many schools that have been closed in the past are still sitting empty. One example is Smith. It's been abandoned, I don't know, something like 19 years. Custodians still have to check on this building daily because of constant break-ins and vandalism. We're still paying to maintain these empty buildings.

It does not make sense to add 10 more empty buildings to the list. Portland taxpayers have paid millions to renovate PPS buildings across the city. We cannot afford to leave these buildings empty. Our members will continue to maintain these buildings, but it still costs us all.

Originally, I signed up to speak because Maplewood was on the closure list. I was very sad because we are like a family there, like every single other school. We're family. I am so happy that Maplewood's no longer on that list, but I'm still so angry that 10 other schools are still on that list.

These proposed closures not only- sorry- affect the educational landscape, but also have broader implications for our neighbors and families. Families rely on schools for more than education. They provide extracurricular activities, social services, and a sense of belonging. Schools are vital community hub. Closing them disrupts local connections and support systems.

You've already heard about the impacts on families, increasing class size, disruption of learning, and the cost of transition. We know that things are not sustainable as they are now. We know we need change. While closures may appear to address immediate deficits, they do not resolve underlying financial shortfalls and would lead to further cuts in programs and staff, which would be very harmful to students in our community. I mentioned the 10 other schools on the closure list, but I want to name them here to make sure that you know they're not just buildings.
They're students. They're staff. They're families. They are community. Irvington, Rose City Park, Buckman, Creston, Marysville, Woodmere, Lewis, Beach, Peninsula, and Sabin.

Each of these schools are a community, and closing even one will deeply impact our PPS families. Until we get accurate, transparent information, we call on the PPS board to consider these negative aspects seriously. Please pause decision-making. Please continue to engage with the community in exploring alternative solutions, which is critical to ensure that our schools remain a source of strength and support for all students and families. Thank you.
Good evening. My name is Elizabeth Held, H-E-L-D. I am the president of PFSP.
I'm here tonight um in part to thank um directors Inglesman and Directors LaFort for your courage last week. We appreciated everything you brought forward.

And I am here tonight to represent some of the concerns that my members have been brought forward about the district- the superintendent's recommendation. We have concerns around receiving schools that don't have gymnasiums. We have concerns around receiving schools that don't have enough classrooms for DLI programming. We have concerns about receiving schools that don't have space for their special education programs. We have been told that the reason that we are doing this is to provide well-resourced schools for our students, but we don't know what real well-resourced schools mean.

We don't know if we will have 2 school administrative assistants at every school. We don't know if we will have educational assistants in kindergarten classrooms. We don't know if we will be able to have libraries open with library assistants inside of them. We are being told that we need to close these schools so that we can serve students, but we don't actually know what we are promising these students in return for these closures.

And it is deeply concerning to my members and to people that I speak to in the community that we are talking about these and talking about making a decision when we don't have these basic answers yet. I would urge the board to wait and to make a decision only after we are able to answer these basic questions about what school closures will mean.
Thank you.

Hello everybody, my name is um Alicia Chavez. I'm a kindergarten through 2nd grade special education teacher um at Atkinson Elementary and a currently serving as the Portland Association of Teachers president. Hello.
